title: Work, Energy & Power (part 1)
textbookText: Chapter 5 Work, Energy & Power The French mathematician Gaspard-Gustave Coriolis introduced the term work in 1826 saying "weight lifted through a height", similar to the case of early steam engines to lift buckets of water out of flooded ore mines. The modern statement: "work is force times path" is due to him and gave the correct formula for change in kinetic energy associated with work although he spoke of force vive (including the modern factor ½), instead of kinetic energy. The word energy is derived from the Greek word ἐνέργεια (energeia) which appears for the first time in the 4th century BCE works of Aristotal. Leibniz defined the product of the mass of an object and its velocity squared from the idea of Vis viva (living force), as a modern concept of the energy. In 1802 lectures to the Royal Society, Thomas Young was the first to use the term energy in its modern sense, instead of Vis viva. The term finally was first invented by him in 1807 after the Greek word Energeia that roughly translates to “activity.” Energy is the ability for an object to perform work on another object”. Moreover, Gustave-Gaspard Coriolis described the term kinetic energy in 1829 in its modern sense, and Thomas Rankine introduced the term potential energy in 1853.

Do or observe the following tasks: i) Visit a bank or some company, or some industrial area, and notice a guard standing at the gate. ii) Visit the fields and watch a farmer digging or ploughing the field. iii) Note some people carrying loads on their backs.

iv) Watch a man lifting a bucket of water and walking along the road. v) Observe a man with loads on his head and walking along. vi) Remember, the people involved in all these tasks receive payment accordingly. Q: Do all these phenomena refer to a specific type of work? If they all imply the act of doing something, what is the definition of this work? In case the nature of the work varies, how would you define work to encompass all these tasks?

In a common sense, all of these tasks exemplify work. However, in physics, the concept of work carries a distinct meaning. Work is defined as the product of a force acting upon a system and the displacement of that system occurring in the direction of the force. Mathematically, work (w) = force (f).displacement (d) i.e, w= f.d If the force acts at an angle θ, then w = fdcosθ For d =0, w = 0 Hence for work to occur, there must be displacement in the direction of the force. If the displacement is zero, no work is done. Therefore, i) A gateman or guard standing all day is often considered as doing no work, as there is no net displacement. ii) A man carrying a load while standing also does not perform any work. iii) Additionally, the work done by static friction exerted by a body on a surface is zero because there is no displacement.

If θ =00, w = fd i.e, they act in the same direction. If θ = 900, w = 0 iv) A man walking while carrying a water bucket does zero work because the load acts vertically downwards while he moves forward. In this case, the load and the displacement are perpendicular, forming a 90-degree angle. According to the formula w = fdcosθ, where θ represents the angle between force and displacement, the cosine of 90 degrees is 0, resulting in zero work being done. v) The work done by the centripetal force around a circle is zero because the force and the displacement act at 90 degrees. vi) The work done by the tension in a string when a body undergoes a circular path is also zero. vii) A coolie carrying a load on his head while traveling on a platform is said to have done zero work. viii) The work done due to the movement of a body on a frictionless surface, when the force (F) is equal to zero, is also zero. But, a porter moving vertically up the stairs with a suitcase on his head does work. Why? → The porter applies the force upwards against the load that is acting vertically downwards. Since the displacement here is in the direction of the force applied by the porter, there is work done.

Units and Dimension of Work: 1 joule=? It is the work done by a force of 1N to produce 1m displacement. i.e, 1 joule = 1N×1m. The joule refers to the name of James, an English physicist.
